{{Orphan|date=March 2018}}
'''Genetic assignment methods''' are powerful [[statistical methods]] used to determine the relationship between individuals and [[Population (biology)|populations]].<ref>Remais, Justin V., et al. "[https://journals.plos.org/plospathogens/article?id=10.1371/journal.ppat.1002013 Genetic assignment methods for gaining insight into the management of infectious disease by understanding pathogen, vector, and host movement]." PLOS Pathogens 7.4 (2011): e1002013.</ref> The general principle behind these methods is to utilize [[multilocus genotype]]s to assign individuals to reference populations based on their origins.<ref>Piry, Sylvain, et al. "[https://academic.oup.com/jhered/article/95/6/536/2187551 GENECLASS2: a software for genetic assignment and first-generation migrant detection]." Journal of heredity 95.6 (2004): 536–539.</ref>

==Genetic assignment methods==
===Frequency method===
This method was first presented by Paetkau et al. in 1995.<ref>Paetkau, D., et al. "[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1365-294X.1995.tb00227.x Microsatellite analysis of population structure in Canadian polar bears]." Molecular ecology 4.3 (1995): 347–354.</ref> It assigns an individual to the reference population based on the [[likelihood]] of that individual's [[genotype]] in the population. This method assumes [[Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium]] and independence of loci, as well as an unstated assumption that is the deduced population sample [[Allele frequency|allelic frequencies]] are close to the exact values.<ref name = "review">Cornuet, Jean-Marie, et al. "[https://www.genetics.org/content/153/4/1989.full-text.pdf+html New methods employing multilocus genotypes to select or exclude populations as origins of individuals]." Genetics 153.4 (1999): 1989–2000.</ref>
This method involves three steps:<ref name = "review" />

# Computing the required allelic frequencies in all candidate populations.
# Computing the likelihoods of the individual's [[multilocus genotype]] occurring in each population.
# Assigning the individual to the population where the likelihood of the individual's [[genotype]] is the highest.

===Bayesian model===
Inspired by Rannala and Mountain,<ref name = "Bayesian">Rannala, Bruce, and Joanna L. Mountain. "[https://www.pnas.org/content/pnas/94/17/9197.full.pdf Detecting immigration by using multilocus genotypes]." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 94.17 (1997): 9197–9201.</ref> this method was presented in their 1997 paper, which emphasized a [[Bayesian approach]] was used to detect [[immigration]]. It assumes that each [[Locus_(genetics)|locus]]’ allelic frequencies in each population have an equal [[prior probability]]. The [[marginal probability]] of observing an individual with genotype <math> \scriptstyle A_k A_{k'} </math> at locus ''j'' in population ''i'' is equal to<ref name = "Bayesian" />

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \frac{\left(\frac{n_{ijk}+1}{K_j+1}\right) \left(\frac{n_{ijk}+1}{K_j}\right)}{(n_{ij}+2)(n_{ij}+1)} & & \text{ for } k = k' \\[6pt]
& \frac{2 \left( \frac{n_{ijk}+1}{K_j} \right) \left( \frac{n_{ijk'}+1}{K_j} \right) }{(n_{ij}+2)(n_{ij}+1)} & & \text{ for } k \neq k'
\end{align}
</math>

''n''<sub>''ijk''</sub> is the number of [[alleles]] ''k'' sampled at locus ''j'' in population ''i'', ''n''<sub>''ij''</sub> is the number of [[gene]] copies sampled at locus ''j'' in population ''i'', and ''kj'' is the total number of [[alleles]] observed in the whole populations at locus&nbsp;''j''.

===Distance method===
Introduced by Cornuet et al. in 1999,<ref name = "review" />  this method uses [[genetic distance]] to assign the individual to the “closest” population. For the interpopulation distances, an individual is assigned as a sample of two [[alleles]]; for shared allele distance, the measure is the average distance between the individual and the population samples. Note this method does not assume [[Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium]] or independence of [[Locus (genetics)|loci]].<ref name = "review"/>
